Tencent Japan  ·  2023–2026  ·  Aostar

Making AI behaviour
legible at scale

Aostar is a mobile social game where players manage a living homeland with AI-driven companion characters called Guangzai. I owned both the AI priority logic and the UX layer that made it visible — designing how autonomous behaviour becomes something players can understand, trust, and act on.

Company
Tencent Japan
Role
Senior UI/UX Designer
Platform
Mobile (iOS & Android)
Year
2023 – 2026
01 — Problem

An intelligent system that felt broken

Guangzai are AI-driven companions that live, work, and have needs inside a player's homeland. Their behaviour is governed by a state machine — invisible to players by default. When a Guangzai stopped working mid-task, wandered off, or collapsed, players had no explanation. Without understanding why, they assumed bugs rather than intelligence. Trust broke down.

The scale made it harder: at full capacity, a player manages up to 20 Guangzai simultaneously, each running independent AI with separate states and priorities. The challenge wasn't designing one character — it was designing legibility across an entire system.

"The AI behaviour was real and working correctly. The design problem was making players feel that — rather than feel abandoned by it."

// Homeland interior — player and Guangzai companion in a furnished home. Furniture placement affects Guangzai needs and behaviours.
02 — What I Owned

Both the logic and the interface

Most UX designers inherit a system and design the surface. Here I owned both. Working with the game design team, I defined the AI priority hierarchy — the rules governing which states take precedence and how urgently players need to respond. I then designed the UX layer that communicated those rules in real time.

This maps directly to the challenge facing any AI product: how do you make autonomous system behaviour legible, trustworthy, and actionable for the people depending on it?

AI Logic

Designed the three-tier priority system governing how Guangzai states are weighted, which states override others, and how the system escalates when needs go unmet.

UX Layer

Designed how each priority level appears in the world — through bubbles, icons, animation, distance-based feedback, and the management interface — so players can read the system at a glance.

03 — The Priority Hierarchy

Three levels. One clear system.

The priority system is the core design decision. With 20 Guangzai running simultaneously, players can't respond to everything. The hierarchy ensures critical states are impossible to miss, while ambient states are safely ignorable — players develop intuition for the system without consciously learning it.

Level Name When it fires Visual treatment
L3 Alert Guangzai or facility in critical state. All tasks stop.
Needs bathroom · Starving · Fainting · Facility at capacity
 Red colour, pulsing animation, prominent bubble. Visible at distance as icon only.
L2 Notice State affects behaviour but not critical.
Hungry · Tired · Dreaming · Facility nearly full
 Elevated icon, mid-level animation. Not shown at distance.
L1 Ambient Normal interaction. No player action required.
Socialising · Resting · Entertainment
 Small subtle icon. No animation. Not shown at distance.
🖼 Priority matrix — L1/L2/L3 urgency vs proximity (near/far)
// Priority matrix — defining what players see at each combination of urgency and distance
04 — Guangzai Character Needs

Making character states readable in the world

Each Guangzai has three core needs — energy, food, and mood — that deplete over time and affect their behaviour. I designed how each state appears in-world at different priority levels, and how the system communicates emotional state through character expression before bars turn critical.

The hardest problem: two states that look visually similar but require completely different responses. Dreaming (L2) — the Guangzai wanders in its sleep, not dangerous. Fainting (L3) — requires immediate player action. The distinction had to be unambiguous or the entire trust model breaks.

"The split between character alerts and facility alerts was a deliberate design decision — players need to know not just that something is wrong, but where the problem actually lives."

06 — Status Screen & Response Flow

From alert to understanding to action

In-world bubbles signal that something is happening. The status screen tells players exactly what, and gives them the tools to respond. I designed the full interaction flow — needs meters, contextual action menus, feeding flows, empty states, and post-action confirmation — so the resolution path is always clear.

🖼 Status screen — energy, food, mood meters + contextual action menu
// Status screen — three need meters at a glance, action menu adapts to current Guangzai state
🖼 Feeding screen — food selected with stats
// Food selected — satiety, buff effect, and quality rating before confirming
🖼 Empty state — no food available
// Empty state — prompts player to cook first, closing the resource loop
🖼 Post-feeding — Guangzai personality dialogue confirms success
// Post-feeding response — personality-driven dialogue makes the interaction feel meaningful, not mechanical
07 — Management System

The full roster view

Players also needed a dedicated overview to see their entire Guangzai roster — who's working, who needs attention, who's available — and make decisions about assignments based on each character's skills, personality, and rarity. I designed the management screen, all slot states, and the full assignment flow.

🖼 Overview screen — daily summary, Guangzai roster with titles, slot count
// Main overview — refreshes daily based on homeland performance data
🖼 Management grid — slot states (occupied, empty, locked, companion)
// Management grid — all slot states scannable at a glance
🖼 Character detail — attributes, skills, personality, assignment
// Character detail — supports informed assignment decisions
08 — Outcomes

What shipped and what it meant

The Guangzai system shipped during beta and became a core differentiator of the Aostar homeland experience. The L1/L2/L3 priority framework became the reference standard for all subsequent state-based UI design across the project.

20
Simultaneous AI characters — each with independent state machines designed to be legible in real time
3
Priority tiers designed from scratch — became the project-wide UX standard for all state-based systems
2×
Ownership — both the AI behaviour logic and the UX layer, an unusually complete product contribution
